topics.topic: Formal invariant and Required-test coverage for record-storage failure, termination, recovery replay, and eventual result
questions: What formal invariant and Required test must show the new record-storage-failure branch, including process termination and execution again during recovery, and must test 11 exclude or inject a failed record write?

What formal invariant and Required tests item show the required stop, absence of a concluded record, recovery replay, attempt-number treatment, and eventual result when the cleanup_failed record cannot be stored?
Must this test assume that the record can be stored, or must it also exercise the newly specified branch where the record cannot be stored?

What formal invariant states the required behavior when storing the cleanup_failed record fails, and which Required tests item must show both that the kernel stops and that the correct element is executed again after restart without creating a duplicate or skipping it?

quotes:
If that record cannot be stored,
   the kernel process stops all the same, and recovery executes the element
   again, as it does every function element without a concluded record.

11. A03-5: When removal of the exchange directory cannot be confirmed, the execution is
    recorded `crashed` with detail `cleanup_failed`, its output is discarded and
    the kernel process stops.
    [witness: verification:kernel_a03_unconfirmed_cleanup_stops_kernel]
judgement.why: The Required test does not mention a failed record write or recovery replay, but no admissible two-outcome witness exists because the normative rule already requires the process to stop and recovery to execute the element again.

topics.topic: Whether an execution with an unstored cleanup-failed record is concluded and how its record and attempt number are handled on replay
questions: Is the cleanup-failed execution whose NodeExecution could not be stored a concluded attempt, and if so how can A15's exactly-one-record invariant coexist with rerunning it?

When cleanup is unconfirmed but the cleanup_failed record cannot be stored, is the completed sandbox execution a concluded attempt that must have its own NodeExecution, or is it declared not concluded and replaced by the recovered execution under the same attempt number?
Is the cleanup_failed execution whose NodeExecution could not be stored a concluded attempt, in which case A15 is false, or an unconcluded attempt that recovery repeats under the same attempt number?

quotes:
If that record cannot be stored,
   the kernel process stops all the same, and recovery executes the element
   again, as it does every function element without a concluded record.

For one run, node and element, `attempt_number` is the ordinal of the
   element's NodeExecution M23 records: each NodeExecution written for the
   element takes the next number, from 1, whatever its status — an execution, a
   send, a pre-send failure, an owner's refusal, a skip, an upstream failure, the
   record of a mapped node over an empty list.
judgement.why: The failed write leaves no concluded record, so recovery repeats the element and the next successfully written NodeExecution takes the next ordinal; the unstored execution takes no attempt number.

topics.topic: Whether and how startup recovery repeats unstored TrialExecutions from admission or explicit try, versus only run elements
questions: Does automatic recovery after an unstorable execution record apply only to function elements of runs, or also to TrialExecutions created by admission or an explicit try, and if it applies to admission does it replace A04's requirement for another submission?

Does start-up recovery automatically repeat an admission TrialExecution whose cleanup-failure record could not be stored, or are trial executions outside “element” recovery and repeated only by a later submission?

Does automatic start-up recovery apply only to function elements of runs, or also to failed-to-record TrialExecutions performed by admission; and if it applies to admission, how does that agree with A04's requirement that after restart a submission runs admission afresh?

What happens when the unstorable cleanup_failed record belongs to an explicit try rather than to a run element: is the trial execution repeated after restart, abandoned, or repeated only by a new try request?

quotes:
Admission executes the implementation on every case of the corpus, in corpus
   order, each as one TrialExecution M07, and never stops early — save for an
   execution whose cleanup cannot be confirmed: it is recorded `crashed` with
   `cleanup_failed` and the kernel stops (A03 rule 7), with no verdict
   recorded; after the restart a submission runs admission afresh.

Trying an implementation (State 0 action), by any agent,
   executes an existing implementation on the cases of its contract version's
   corpus that the request names, all of them when it names none, in corpus
   order, records one TrialExecution per case and returns them.

On start, before the surface accepts a request, the kernel turns every
   `in_flight` EffectAttempt into `unknown` (A11 rule 4) and then derives every
   run that has not ended — `running`, `awaiting_approval` or `pending` — again
   from its records, oldest first in store order, rewriting a stored status or
   waiting point that lags them (a decided approval, a resolved attempt, an
   outcome whose run change was lost), and advances, as the
   kernel actor, every run that derivation leaves `running`: a
   function element without a
   concluded record is executed again, which is safe because it has no effect; a `read`
   element without one is sent again; an operation element of another class with
   neither a concluded record nor an EffectAttempt was never sent and is advanced
   as if reached for the first time — an approved, unused approval covers it
   only while the rebuilt request has its `request_digest` (A10 rules 1 and 7).
judgement.why: Automatic startup replay is defined for function elements of unfinished runs; admission resumes only through a later submission, and an explicit try is repeated only by another try request.

questions: What exact representation does `clock_module.now` return and records use: timezone, UTC normalization, precision, resolution, serialization form, and treatment of leap seconds or ambiguous local times?

questions: Replace the generic “one clock module” delivery statement with an explicit `time_source_policy` delivered through the IR `system_clock_backend`, while retaining the behavioral rule that no other module reads wall time.

topics.topic: Required cleanup or proof of removal of the old sandbox environment before recovery replay
questions: Before executing the element again, must start-up recovery prove that the old sandbox processes and exchange directory are gone, clean them itself, or may it retry while the earlier environment remains unconfirmed?

quotes: execute_function: [SECURITY_BOUNDARY] Agent code is untrusted: it MUST only ever run inside a fresh bubblewrap environment created for that one execution, never in the kernel process and never through a faster path, and the environment never receives a credential (A03 rule 1, decision 25).

execute_function: [SECURITY_BOUNDARY] MUST start bubblewrap with new user, PID, IPC, UTS and network namespaces and no network interface but the new namespace's own loopback, which bubblewrap brings up, with no capability option, the environment cleared and then set exactly to the imported SANDBOX_ENVIRONMENT constant, exactly the host paths of the imported SANDBOX_RUNTIME_PATHS constant bound read-only, inside the new root the symbolic links of the imported SANDBOX_ROOT_SYMLINKS constant (each name linking to its target, made by bubblewrap --symlink), one fresh private exchange directory bound read-write, bubblewrap's own fresh proc mounted at the imported SANDBOX_PROC_MOUNT constant and minimal dev mounts, and no other host directory; the child dies with its parent, and the runner is the init of the new PID namespace (bubblewrap --as-pid-1), so bubblewrap exits only after the host kernel has killed and reaped every other process of that namespace. The interpreter it starts there is os.path.realpath(sys.executable), the kernel's own CPython under a path of the imported SANDBOX_RUNTIME_PATHS constant, never a launcher such as a virtual environment's.

run_start_sequence: [ORCHESTRATION] MUST call, in exactly this order and each exactly once: load_installation with config_path; check_installed_instances with the loaded Installation; open_store with that Installation's data_directory; probe_sandbox; recover_in_flight_attempts; recover_running_runs (A03 rule 8, A09 rule 1, A14 rule 5, A18).
judgement.why: The later module notes require the old sandbox child to die with the kernel process, then run the exact startup sequence and replay in a fresh environment and exchange directory without an additional old-environment proof step.

topics.topic: Response to the in-flight request before termination after its execution record cannot be stored
questions: Before the kernel process stops, what response, if any, does the request whose execution lost its record receive?

judgement.why: P2 already decided the same question on unchanged text: the request receives an internal-error response before the surface ends the process.

precedent.topic: Whether the triggering request receives a response after cleanup failure
quotes:
It returns the stop to its caller, and
  `surface` ends the process: during a request after answering it as an
  internal error (A16 rule 7), during the start by stopping the start.
precedent.why: The module design decides that a request is answered as an internal error before the surface ends the process.

topics.topic: Type, units, arithmetic, and deadline comparison for monotonic time
questions: What type, unit and arithmetic represent monotonic readings and deadlines, and which comparison decides that a deadline has passed?

quotes:
**Time** is `KernelInstant` (`epoch_us`, integer microseconds since the Unix
  epoch, UTC), the one representation of every recorded `*_at` field;
  `clock.kernel_now` returns it. `clock.monotonic_ns` returns one raw host
  monotonic reading in nanoseconds (`int`); a bounded wait derives its deadline
  from it and keeps it in memory only, never stored (A19 rule 2; decision 26).

A bounded
      wait reads `monotonic_ns` once at its start; its deadline is that
      reading plus the bound in nanoseconds, held in a local variable of the
      waiting function only and never stored (A19 rule 2); the wait has
      passed when a later reading reaches it, and the time left is the
      difference rounded up to whole milliseconds (convention 15).
judgement.why: The later contract fixes monotonic readings as integer nanoseconds, the deadline as the initial reading plus the converted bound, and expiry when a later reading reaches the deadline, equivalent to `now >= deadline`.

topics.topic: Wall-clock read count and timestamp reuse within one operation
questions: How many wall-clock readings may one operation take, and which records or fields created by the same operation must reuse one reading rather than call `now` independently?

judgement.why: P5 already judged the same wall-clock read-count and timestamp-reuse question on unchanged passages.

precedent.topic: Number and reuse of wall-clock readings within an operation
quotes:
Every timestamp the kernel records comes from one clock module; no other part
   of the kernel reads the wall clock. A request never supplies the current time.

Deadlines of one sandbox execution and one HTTP request are measured with the
   monotonic clock of the same module; a monotonic reading is never stored.
precedent.why: These clock-reading rules are unchanged from the closed text, and the transition did not alter when readings are taken or reused.
